Thyroid follicles.description: Thyroid follicles are hollow spheres lined by a single layer of follicular cells and filled with colloid, a thyroglobulin-rich store where thyroid hormones are made and kept. The follicular cells take colloid back in by endocytosis, break it down and release T3 and T4 into the blood. Parafollicular C cells, found between the follicles, make calcitonin instead of thyroid hormone.
clinical: In Graves disease, antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor make the follicular cells grow and overproduce hormone. The follicles then show tall cells, and the colloid often has scalloped edges where the cells have taken it back in.
In Hashimoto thyroiditis the immune system attacks the gland, with lymphocytes infiltrating the tissue and destroying follicles, so the gland often becomes underactive.

Capsule & stroma.description: A fibrous capsule wraps the thyroid and sends thin septa into the gland. Fine reticular connective tissue fills the spaces between follicles, holding them in place and carrying blood vessels and nerves.
clinical: Riedel thyroiditis is a rare condition in which dense fibrous tissue replaces normal thyroid tissue and can spread into the neck around the gland. The thyroid then feels hard and woody and may press on nearby structures.

Thyroid vessels.description: The thyroid is richly supplied with blood by the superior and inferior thyroid arteries, and a dense capillary network surrounds each follicle. Blood leaves through the thyroid veins, carrying released hormones into the circulation.
clinical: Risk to the voice nerve in thyroid surgery

The inferior thyroid artery runs close to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which controls most of the voice box muscles. Surgeons take care when they tie off this artery during thyroid surgery, because nerve injury can cause a hoarse voice.

Parathyroid specimen.description: The parathyroid glands are usually four small glands lying behind the thyroid. They make parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium, and their cells form solid cords and clusters rather than fluid-filled follicles. Most cells are chief cells, which make PTH; oxyphil cells are larger and rich in mitochondria, and their exact function is not well understood.
clinical: Most cases are caused by a single benign tumor (adenoma) of parathyroid cells that makes too much PTH. The excess hormone raises blood calcium, which can lead to kidney stones and bone loss.
The parathyroid glands lie behind the thyroid, so they can be damaged or removed during thyroid surgery. Without enough PTH, blood calcium falls, which causes tingling and muscle cramps.

parts.description: The follicular epithelium is the single layer of cuboidal (cube-shaped) follicular cells that lines the wall of each thyroid follicle. These cells trap iodide, make thyroglobulin (a large protein that stores the hormones), and release thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) into the surrounding capillaries. In a section it forms a ring of small cells around the central colloid, becoming taller and more columnar when the gland is highly active.

Colloid is the thick, pink-staining fluid that fills the central lumen (cavity) of each thyroid follicle. It is mainly thyroglobulin, a large protein made by the follicular cells, to which iodine is attached to form the hormones T3 and T4 that are stored there until needed. In a section it forms a homogeneous pink mass in the middle of each follicle, and it is usually abundant in quiet glands but reduced in highly active ones.

The follicular basal lamina is the thin sheet of extracellular matrix (part of the basement membrane) that lies between the base of the follicular cells and the connective tissue around each follicle. It is made of collagen type IV and laminin, which anchor the epithelium and help give the follicle its shape. In routine light microscopy it is hard to see, appearing only as a faint, thin line at the outer edge of the follicular cells, though special stains can make it clearer.

The follicular cell nuclei are the nuclei of the follicular cells that line each thyroid follicle. Each cell has one nucleus, so the nuclei form a single row around the colloid. In a quiet follicle the cells are low and the nuclei are round and central, whereas in an active follicle the cells are taller and the nuclei are oval and sit nearer the base of the cell, which helps judge how active the gland is.

Intracellular colloid uptake vesicles are small droplets of colloid that follicular cells have taken in by endocytosis, the process by which a cell engulfs material in a membrane-bound bubble. They sit at the lumen-facing top of the cell, and once inside they fuse with lysosomes, whose enzymes cut thyroglobulin apart so that T3 and T4 can be released into the blood. In a section they appear as pink droplets near the top of the cells, most numerous when the gland is active.

Parafollicular C cells are large, pale hormone-secreting cells that make calcitonin, a hormone that lowers blood calcium by reducing bone breakdown. They lie between the follicles, in the connective tissue or in the wall of a follicle, but do not reach the colloid-filled lumen. In a section they look paler and larger than the neighbouring follicular cells, and they are usually seen as single cells or small groups. Medullary thyroid carcinoma, a rare cancer of these cells, releases large amounts of calcitonin.

C-cell nuclei are the nuclei of parafollicular C cells, the calcitonin-producing cells that lie between the thyroid follicles. Each C cell has one round or oval nucleus within its larger, paler cell body, and that body does not reach the colloid-filled lumen. In a section they are found in the connective tissue between follicles or in the outer part of a follicle wall, not among the cells that line the colloid.

Interfollicular connective tissue is the loose connective tissue (stroma) that fills the spaces between neighbouring thyroid follicles. It contains a fine network of reticular fibres (thin collagen type III strands), fibroblasts, capillaries and nerves, which hold the follicles in place and carry the blood vessels that supply each one. In a section it appears as a pale, lacy network between the follicles, and it is where parafollicular C cells often lie.

The thyroid capsule is the thin, dense sheath of fibrous connective tissue that surrounds the whole gland. Fine septa (partitions) run from the capsule into the gland, carrying blood vessels and nerves and dividing the tissue into incomplete lobules. In a section it appears as a pale, dense band of collagen at the outer edge of the thyroid, lying between the gland and the neck tissues around it.

The parathyroid capsule is the thin layer of dense connective tissue that encloses each parathyroid gland and separates it from the surrounding fat and thyroid tissue. Fine septa (partitions) from the capsule carry blood vessels into the gland and divide it into incomplete lobules. In a section it appears as a thin, pale band of collagen at the outer edge of the gland, just outside the cell cords (strands of cells).

The parathyroid stroma is the supporting connective tissue of the gland, made of fine reticular fibres, fibroblasts (connective tissue cells) and a rich capillary network. It fills the spaces between the cords and clusters of parathyroid cells, holding them in place while bringing the blood supply the gland needs to release PTH (parathyroid hormone). In older adults the stroma contains more fat cells, which is a normal age-related change.

Parathyroid chief cells (principal cells) are the main secretory cells of the parathyroid gland, making parathyroid hormone (PTH), which raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and, indirectly, the gut. They are small, polygonal cells arranged in cords and sheets, with a round central nucleus and pale or lightly stained cytoplasm. Because they are the most numerous cells in the gland, they are the cells you see most often when identifying parathyroid tissue.

Oxyphil cells are larger, rounded cells with abundant deeply acidophilic (pink-staining) cytoplasm packed with mitochondria. They occur in clusters or nests within the parathyroid gland, appearing after puberty and increasing in number with age. Their function is not well understood, but their strong pink staining makes them easy to tell apart from the paler chief cells.

Parathyroid adipocytes are fat cells (adipocytes) scattered through the stroma between the parathyroid cell cords. Each one contains a single large droplet of fat that pushes its nucleus and thin rim of cytoplasm to the edge of the cell, and their number rises with age. In a section they appear as large, pale, empty-looking spaces among the parathyroid cells, because the fat is dissolved away during routine preparation.

Parathyroid chief-cell nuclei are the nuclei of the chief cells, the main hormone-making cells of the parathyroid. Each chief cell has one round nucleus near its centre, and these nuclei are fairly uniform in size and shape. Packed into cords (strands) of cells, their regular, round outlines help you recognise parathyroid tissue, which lacks the follicles seen in the thyroid.

Oxyphil-cell nuclei are the nuclei of oxyphil cells, the large cells with deeply pink (acidophilic) cytoplasm that form clusters within the parathyroid gland. Each oxyphil cell has one round nucleus, set in cytoplasm so crowded with mitochondria (energy-producing organelles) that it stains strongly. Finding the pink clusters first makes these nuclei easier to recognise, because they sit among much paler chief cells.

Parathyroid adipocyte nuclei are the nuclei of the fat cells scattered through the parathyroid stroma. Because each fat cell is filled by one large droplet of fat, its nucleus is squeezed into a thin, flattened crescent at the cell edge, giving a signet-ring (ring-shaped) outline. Spotting these flattened, peripheral nuclei beside empty-looking spaces is a reliable way to recognise fat cells in the gland.

Parathyroid lipid droplets are the fat droplets stored inside parathyroid adipocytes (fat cells). Each droplet is a single large mass of triglyceride (stored fat) that fills most of its cell, and it appears as an empty, unstained space because solvents used in routine preparation dissolve the fat. Droplets become more common in older glands, as the number of fat cells increases with age.

Oxyphil mitochondria are the very numerous mitochondria (the energy-producing organelles of the cell) packed through the cytoplasm of oxyphil cells. Their crowding is what makes oxyphil cytoplasm so strongly acidophilic (pink-staining) in routine sections. Under the electron microscope they appear as densely packed organelles with many internal folds called cristae.

The parathyroid circulation is the blood supply and venous drainage of the parathyroid glands, which comes mainly from the inferior thyroid arteries, with a smaller contribution from the superior thyroid arteries. A dense capillary network surrounds the cords of parathyroid cells, and blood leaves through veins that drain into the thyroid veins. This rich supply lets each gland release parathyroid hormone straight into the bloodstream.
